In brief

In the final two chapters of Ulysses both Blooms recall a couple whom they knew early in their marriage, the Comerfords. If these were real people almost nothing is known about them. Annotators have identified a married couple in Dalkey with the same name but ventured no reasons that the Blooms might have been friendly with them. A more intriguing possibility is that the Comerfords lived in the same heavily Jewish south-central Dublin neighborhood where the Blooms lived in the early 1890s. If so, then the novel may be offering a brief glimpse of friendly relations between Jews and Protestants—an interesting counterpoint to Bloom's current uneasy relationships with Dublin's Catholics.

At more length

The drawer that Bloom unlocks in Ithaca contains "a Yuletide card, bearing on it a pictorial representation of a parasitic plant, the legend Mizpah, the date Xmas 1892, the name of the senders: from Mr and Mrs M. Comerford, the versicle: May this Yuletide bring to thee, Joy and peace and welcome glee." The Comerfords are mentioned again in Penelope when Molly is thinking about Dublin's streetside male urinals. She recalls "coming home with Poldy after the Comerfords party oranges and lemonade to make you feel nice and watery I went into 1 of them it was so biting cold I couldnt keep it when was that 93 the canal was frozen yes it was a few months after a pity a couple of the Camerons werent there to see me squatting in the mens place meadero." Meadero is a Spanish word for urinals sometimes applied to the kinds of multi-occupant pissoirs known as "greenhouses" in Dublin.

Picture postcards sent at Christmastime, which Gifford notes were introduced into London society in 1846, became hugely popular in the UK and the US in the last few decades of the century. Mistletoe, "a parasitic plant," was featured on many such Christmas cards—sometimes by itself, sometimes entwined with the similarly evergreen holly, and sometimes hanging over the heads of kissing couples. "Mizpah," also featured on some Victorian and Edwardian cards (though not on any Christmas cards that I have seen), was a popular sentimental greeting based on Genesis 31:49: "And Mizpah; for he said, The Lord watch between me and thee, when we are absent from one another." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner quote from Mary Maillard's Whispers of Cruel Wrongs (2017): "The Victorian concept of Mizpah captured all aspects of absence, from temporary separation to final parting in death" (15).

The manufacturer of the Blooms' card has evidently combined these two elements and added a seasonal "versicle" whose rhymes ("thee," "glee") echo the "me and thee" of the Mizpah verse. Many cards of the 1890s carried such little verses. The one shown here features four short lines whose B rhymes ("opportunity," "impunity") end with the same sound. The Mizpah greeting was used by many people, not just Jews, but the Comerfords' choice of a card sporting this Hebrew word may suggest that they were reaching across ethnic lines during the Christian holiday. In this connection it may be significant that the card mentions only "Yuletide" and "Xmas," not the name Christ. It may also be significant that Bloom has held onto the card for more than a decade—he would seem to have fond memories of these people.

In late 1892 and early 1893 the Blooms were living on Lombard Street West, not far from "no 52 Clanbrassil street," identified in Ithaca as the address at which Bloom grew up. At that time (and throughout the first half of the 20th century) Clanbrassil Street was the heart of Dublin's Jewish community, composed mostly of refugees from eastern Europe and their descendants. The mention of Comerford, a distinctly English name, has puzzled commentators. John Henry Raleigh (1977) remarks that "This Anglo, somewhat toffish name, is meant to suggest, I believe, that the Blooms had some friends rather higher on the social scale than previous or subsequent to their Lombard West days" (122). Gifford (1988) appears to agree, noting that a couple by this name "Lived at Neptune View, 11 Leslie Avenue, Dalkey, according to Thom's 1904," and Slote (2022) repeats the claim. Dalkey was and is far more "toffish" than Clanbrassil Street, and far removed from it.

But the claim seems problematic, and not only because of the seeming disparity in social class. It is based on the 1904 edition of Thom's directory, more than ten years later than the events in question, and it puts the Comerfords in Dalkey, which is nearly ten miles away from Clanbrassil Street. The considerable distance might account for the Comerfords sending the Blooms a card expressing affection "when we are absent from one another," but it raises the question—never answered in the novel—of how the two couples might have known each other. Gifford does not address this question, or defend the use of a 1904 publication, but he does offer some thoughts about geography, noting that just before thinking of the party Molly has recalled passing "outside the mens greenhouse near the Harcourt street station." The terminus of the Dublin, Wicklow, and Wexford Railway was in Harcourt Street, and he figures that "The Blooms would have come up from Dalkey" on one of its trains. His unstated implication is that Molly, shortly after getting off the train, used the nearby urinal to empty her bladder.

Molly's words do not neatly fit this interpretation, however. Harcourt Street enters her thoughts when she muses on exhibitionists holding out their penises for women to see and recalls many such unpleasant incidents that have happened outside the urinal in that street. But then, in a slight shift of subject, she thinks more generally of "those rotten places," and only after that does she recall "coming home with Poldy after the Comerfords party oranges and lemonade to make you feel nice and watery I went into 1 of them it was so biting cold I couldnt keep it when was that 93 the canal was frozen." It seems unlikely that "1 of them" could refer to the greenhouse named so precisely moments before. And she associates the experience with a frozen canal—not with Harcourt Street, its station, or the train.

The Jewish neighborhood centered on Clanbrassil Street lay just north of the Grand Canal. As he was revising Penelope Joyce referred to their proximity in a 2 November 1921 letter to his Aunt Sara: "Do you remember the cold February of 1893. I think you were in Clanbrassil street. I want to know whether the canal was frozen and if there was any skating." Isn't it possible, then, that the greenhouse in which Molly found relief was located nearby, perhaps at the intersection of Clanbrassil Street and the South Circular Road? This would eliminate the sole textual support for believing that the Comerfords lived in Dalkey.

Patrick Comerford, an Anglican priest descended from Comerfords in County Kilkenny, has advanced a strong alternative reading. By cross-referencing genealogical records with listings in Thom's directory, he has determined that many Comerfords were living in the vicinity of Clanbrassil Street at the turn of the 20th century. In a 25 December 2023 post at www.patrickcomerford.com, he mentions many family members who lived nearby, all of them descendants or other close relatives of his great-grandfather James Comerford (1817-1902), a prominent plasterer, stucco artist, and architect who helped to turn the Dublin plasterers' guild into a trade union.

Comerford sums up the findings of his research: "In the short space of a half century or so, immediate members of this one branch of the Comerford family had addresses in at least 15 houses in Lower and Upper Clanbrassil Street, and many more lived in the warren of streets off Clanbrassil Street, in Little Jerusalem, in Portobello and around Charlemont Street. If I add their in-laws, their cousins and their nieces and nephews, it must have been impossible then to walk along Clanbrassil Street without meeting and greeting a member of the Comerford family." Oral tradition passed down in the family held that "every second person on Lower Clanbrassil Street then was either a Jew or a Comerford."

Patrick Comerford's research provides a hefty counterweight to the single bare mention of a "Mr and Mrs M Comerford" living in Dalkey. But that pesky "M" poses a challenge. Some of the female Comerfords he identifies as living on or near Clanbrassil Street in the 1890s had given names beginning with M, but none of the men. This does not necessarily refute the theory. The name could be fictive: not every person in the novel other than the Blooms is based on someone real, and this seems particularly true of incidental, non-speaking characters like the Comerfords. And even if Joyce did get the surname from Thom's, a certain amount of caution is advisable when dealing with its initials. In Calypso Bloom remembers a Jewish couple called the "Citrons" who lived in the same neighborhood, and "J. Citron" makes an appearance in Circe. The name comes from Thom's, but Louis Hyman has shown that the real man's given name was Israel.

In that case Joyce faithfully reproduced someone else's mistaken substitution of a similar-looking capital letter. But there are also probably instances of his creatively altering what he found in Thom's, or not consulting it at all. The bartender called "Terence O'Ryan" in Barney Kiernan's pub prompts Gifford (followed, again, by Slote) to claim that Joyce is giving him the name of a Roman Catholic priest named Terence W. O'Ryan, implicitly punning on his role as a "curate." But at that particular moment in Cyclops Joyce is parodying the contemporary Irish enthusiasm for noble ancient names beginning in O' (in the same parodic section, Alf Bergan becomes "the young chief of the O'Bergans"). The real-life model, then, if there was one, may have been named simply Ryan. And in this case why would Joyce have needed to crack open Thom's? The bartender is an exceedingly minor, almost anonymous, character, elsewhere (21 times in all) called only "Terry."

More interesting, perhaps, than the search for two real people and a precise address is Joyce's decision to extend the Blooms' social circle from Jews like Citron, Mastiansky, and Moisel to some of the Comerfords who lived in their midst. Bloom's family story is one of religious assimilation. His immigrant father accepted conversion to the Church of Ireland in 1865 and raised his son nominally as an Anglican while quietly laboring at home to instill in him a strong Jewish heritage. In 1888 the son became nominally Catholic in order to marry the half-Jewish but doctrinally Catholic Marion Tweedy. None of his religious affiliations—Jewish, Catholic, Anglican—have mattered very much to Bloom in a spiritual sense. Socially, however, they hold considerable importance.

The novel shows Bloom working hard in 1904, and more often than not failing, to gain the trust of Dublin's middle-class Catholics. Earlier he had many Jewish friends in his community of origin but he has since drifted away from them, with some concomitant guilt. It seems that he also had at least two Protestant friends, whether acquired as a result of his involvement in the Irish church or simply because they were neighbors. The Jews and Anglicans prominent in this part of town were minorities in heavily Catholic Dublin, and Joyce's decision to associate them via the Christmas card and the party may be significant, since after making the hero of Ulysses a Jew he centered Finnegans Wake on a Protestant pubowner. The theme of the outsider runs strong in his novels.

One additional shred of significance may possibly lurk in Joyce's decision to reference the Comerfords of Little Jerualem. Patrick Comerford suggests that he may have included them in his book to honor John Comerford, a Kilkenny-born painter of miniatures. Family portraits were important to John Stanislaus Joyce, and they remained important to his son James. Ellmann notes that Joyce added Patrick Tuohy's spirited portrait of his father "to the group of family portraits by William Roe, which he in turn carried about from flat to flat in later life" (11-12). He adds in an endnote that "Stanislaus Joyce thought the paintings were by Roe, but, according to Arthur Power, James Joyce used to say they were by John Comerford" (746). 

The curators of the James Joyce Collection at SUNY Buffalo agree with the writer. They attribute their five portraits of his family members—his paternal great-grandfather, paternal great-grandmother, paternal grandfather (2), and paternal grandmother—to John Comerford. There seems to be a problem with this attribution, as they date the five portraits to the 1840s and 50s but Comerford died in 1832. Even if the portraits were painted by William Roe, however, that would not alter the value that Joyce attached to the name of Comerford.

John Hunt 2026
